program_meta.program_name: MSc Computer Science, Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Mathematics and Computer Science (EEMCS/EWI). No track literally named 'Intelligent Systems' exists inside the MSc CS programme itself - 'Intelligent Systems' (INSY) is the EEMCS DEPARTMENT that co-runs CS (with Software Technology dept) and supplies most of the AI/ML faculty. The programme's own themes (choose 2 of 3-course each) are: Algorithmics, Computer Graphics, Computer Systems, Cyber Security, Distributed Systems Engineering, Information Management, Quantum Computer Science, Software Engineering - none is literally 'AI' or 'Machine Learning', so an ML-focused student picks Information Management or Algorithmics as the closest formal theme and reaches AI faculty mainly through the thesis/advisor route, not a themed track. SEPARATE DEGREE, NOT A TRACK OF CS: 'MSc Data Science and Artificial Intelligence Technology' (DSAIT), a joint TU Delft programme, is administratively distinct with its own admission page - this is almost certainly what 'DSAIT track' in the brief refers to; it is its own MSc, not an Intelligent-Systems track inside CS. Both CS and DSAIT are on TU Delft's GRE-required programme list (see gre field).
program_meta.degree_target: MSc, with MS->PhD progression via TU Delft's own PhD programme (advertised positions) or via the graduate's own initiative after graduating; TU Delft PhDs are salaried employee positions (not a stipend-based US-style admission), applied for as individual vacancies, typically after the MSc thesis.
program_meta.sop_limit: Called 'Motivation letter', VERBATIM required content and length from the official Required Documents page: 'A clear and relevant essay in English (1,000 - 1,500 words) addressing the following: Your motivation for choosing this MSc programme. Why you are interested in TU Delft and what you expect to find here. If this MSc programme has specialisation(s), which specialisation interests you the most and why? Describe your hypothetical thesis project: what kind of project would you prefer? What would you want to explore? Please limit your answer to three possible topics. Summarize in a maximum of 250 words your BSc thesis work or final assignment/project. Please include information about the workload.' This is a structured, multi-part essay, not a free-form SOP - the 'name faculty you want to work with' function is served by the 'describe your hypothetical thesis project' sub-question.
program_meta.extra_essays: None beyond the motivation letter and CV. An extensive CV (max 3 pages, Europass-style acceptable, must list personal info / work experience / education, newest to oldest) is separately required. Reference letters are NOT required for standard admission - VERBATIM: 'Only required for applicants applying for a scholarship listed on our website' (two letters, from a professor/assistant professor or employer). Portfolio only applies to design programmes (not CS/DSAIT).

So Akshat's MAHE degree does NOT qualify him for exemption; he needs TOEFL/IELTS/Cambridge regardless of English-medium instruction.

faculty.rank: Associate Professor (Head of the Computer Vision Lab)

faculty.research_areas: Data-efficient and data-efficient deep learning; visual inductive priors; equivariance and scale-space theory in CNNs; empirical/understanding-based deep learning research (controlled ablations to explain WHY an improvement happens, not just that it does); action/video recognition; recently holds an NWO VICI grant ('dAIta: Data Efficient AI Foundation Models') and an NWO VIDI ('Tabula Inscripta: adding prior knowledge to deep learning').
faculty.why_match: Van Gemert's entire stated research identity - VERBATIM on his homepage: 'I am an empiricist and do understanding-based research, this means that I ask for (controlled) experiments that validate each step along the way; and search for experimental evidence to try to understand and motivate why a possible improvement happens, and why and when it does not' - is precisely the method Akshat used in the polyp study: holding architecture fixed across three backbones (U-Net, ResU-Net, Attention U-Net) and isolating the preprocessing contribution alone, finding it shrinks from +0.058 to +0.023 Dice as the architecture strengthens. Van Gemert's 2025 CVPR paper 'Making Every Event Count: Balancing Data Efficiency and Accuracy in Event Camera Subsampling' and his long VIPriors workshop series ask exactly this question - how much data/compute can be removed before performance degrades, and what prior knowledge substitutes for it - which is the mirror image of Akshat's diffusion-pretraining result (a learned prior transfers for liver but not kidney).

faculty.key_paper_2: End-to-End Implicit Neural Representations for Classification. CVPR, 2025. (See also: NWO VICI grant 'dAIta: Data Efficient AI Foundation Models', awarded 2025; VIPriors workshop series, ECCV/ICCV 2020-2024.)

faculty.department: EEMCS - Intelligent Systems - Pattern Recognition & Bioinformatics (Pattern Recognition Laboratory)
faculty.research_areas: Methodology and applications of statistical machine learning: semi-supervised learning (his PhD topic - robust methods guaranteed, with high probability, to not perform worse than the fully supervised baseline), causal inference, model evaluation/selection, domain adaptation, philosophy of statistics/data science.
faculty.why_match: Krijthe's PhD work is the theoretical mirror of Akshat's empirical semi-supervised spine-MRI result: Akshat's teacher trained on 54 labelled images produced a student at 0.816 mIoU via confidence + MC-dropout-filtered pseudo-labels (+8.1 points over the teacher), but unfiltered pseudo-labelling barely moved the needle (0.737-0.740) - i.e. the filter is what makes semi-supervised learning safe rather than harmful. Krijthe's dissertation and follow-on work is explicitly about proving WHEN a semi-supervised method is guaranteed not to hurt versus when it can silently degrade performance, which is exactly the risk Akshat's per-class confidence thresholds and MC-dropout filter were built to manage by hand rather than by guarantee.
faculty.key_paper_1: Robust Semi-Supervised Learning (PhD dissertation topic and associated papers: 'safe' semi-supervised classifiers guaranteed to not underperform the supervised baseline), Delft University of Technology.
faculty.key_paper_2: Applications and implicit assumptions in dementia risk scores: A scoping review of the LIBRA score. Co-authored with Marco Loog, 2026 (recent, demonstrates continued active output and an applied-risk-modelling angle relevant to interest E).

faculty.research_areas: Foundations of pattern recognition and learning theory: generalization performance and learning curves, sample-wise monotonicity of learning algorithms, dynamics of randomly initialized deep ReLU networks, classifier evaluation methodology.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's calibration-efficiency finding - that per-class pseudo-label confidence thresholds calibrated on just 5 reference images match those derived from 304 - is an empirical learning-curve statement: performance/behaviour saturates far earlier than the full dataset size would suggest. Loog's 2026 papers 'Generalization performance distributions along learning curves' and (with Tax and Viering) the broader learning-curve research programme formalise exactly this question - how generalization behaves as a function of sample size, and how early a curve's shape can be predicted - which would give Akshat's ad hoc 5-vs-304 calibration observation a theoretical home.

faculty.key_paper_2: On Sample-Wise Strict Monotonicity with a Gradient Update. O. Taylan Turan, Marco Loog, David M.J. Tax, 2026. (See also: The Vanishing Empirical Variance in Randomly Initialized Deep ReLU Networks, 2026; Applications and implicit assumptions in dementia risk scores: A scoping review of the LIBRA score, with Jesse Krijthe, 2026.)

faculty.department: EEMCS - Intelligent Systems - Pattern Recognition & Bioinformatics (Pattern Recognition Laboratory)
faculty.research_areas: Learning curves and generalization behaviour, hyperparameter optimization (early discarding/stopping), safety in machine learning, and - most recently - ML applications to malware evolution analysis with a cybersecurity co-author.
faculty.why_match: Akshat's cross-cutting negative result - a frozen diffusion encoder retains >80% of fine-tuned performance on liver but falls BELOW random initialization on kidney - is exactly the kind of surprising, direction-dependent learning-curve/transfer behaviour Viering's group studies formally. His 2023 paper 'LCDB 1.0: An Extensive Learning Curves Database for Classification Tasks' and 2024 paper on 'early discarding after one epoch' are about predicting when a training/transfer trajectory will succeed or fail early, which is the diagnostic tool that was missing when Akshat's kidney transfer silently failed.
faculty.key_paper_1: LCDB 1.0: An Extensive Learning Curves Database for Classification Tasks. Felix Mohr, Tom J. Viering, Marco Loog, Jan N. van Rijn, 2023.
